periods.activity_title: Drawing and Sharing Our Favourite Foods
periods.textbook_anchor: My Favourite Food — Draw pictures of your favourite homemade food dishes and name them (p. 100)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites children to think silently about one homemade dish they love — its smell, colour, and taste. A few students share aloud to warm the class up.

Students open Textbook p. 100 and draw two or three of their favourite homemade food dishes in their notebooks, writing the name of each dish below its drawing. The teacher circulates, asking gentle questions: 'What colour is it? Is it sweet or spicy?'

In pairs, students share their drawings and explain why they like each dish. The teacher then opens a brief whole-class conversation: children notice that different classmates have drawn very different dishes, and the class collects the tastes named — sweet, sour, spicy, bitter — on the board.

The teacher introduces the idea of Chhappan Bhog — a festive offering of 56 food items representing six different tastes — through a short storytelling moment, inviting children to wonder: 'Which taste is missing from our board?' Students close by adding any missing taste words to their notebooks beside their drawings.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express personal food preferences and describe food variety using sensory attributes such as taste, colour, and smell.
periods.section_context: Drawing and naming favourite homemade dishes, sharing reasons for preferences, six tastes (sweet, sour, spicy, bitter), Chhappan Bhog tradition of 56 food items.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did anyone's family prepare a special food for a festival or a celebration — what was it, and why was it made that day?' This draws out the tradition of festive foods naturally in conversation.

periods.activity_title: Shirin's Food Story — Ticking a Balanced Variety
periods.textbook_anchor: Story of Shirin — the Runner — Why do we need to eat healthy food? (p. 103)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figures accompanying the Shirin story

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the story of Shirin aloud with expression, pausing to let children predict: 'Why do you think Shirin keeps falling sick?' Students listen and look at Textbook p. 103.

The class discusses together: 'Why do we need to eat healthy food?' Children contribute ideas — strength, not falling sick, growing well — and the teacher notes key food groups on the board: vegetables, fruits, grains (rice, ragi, jowar, wheat, bajra), pulses, nuts.

Students tick the food items in the textbook list that they eat regularly, then look at their ticks and discuss in pairs: 'Are you eating a good variety — like Shirin learned to do?' The teacher asks: 'Which food on the list have you never tried? Where do you think it comes from?'

Brief whole-class share: a few children name one food group they would like to try more of. The teacher closes by linking Shirin's improvement to variety — 'It wasn't one magic food; it was many different kinds working together.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain why eating a variety of food groups contributes to physical well-being, using evidence from a narrative example.
periods.section_context: Shirin's story of frequent illness and recovery, ticking regularly eaten food items, balanced diet including vegetables, fruits, multiple grains, pulses, and nuts.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone in your family ever told you to eat something you didn't like because it was good for you — what was it?' This connects health advice from home to the idea of a varied diet without prescribing specific items.

periods.activity_title: Seasonal Foods and Where Food Comes From
periods.section_ref: We Eat Different Things / Where does food come from?
periods.textbook_anchor: Where does food come from? — Do you know which foods are grown in the fields? Write a few names of such crops (p. 105)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figures showing plant parts and animal-based food sources (p. 105)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a quick oral round: 'Name one food you eat more in summer and one you eat more in winter.' Children share freely. The teacher notes a few examples on the board — cool drinks and juicy fruits for summer, warm soups for winter — drawing out that nature's seasons shape what we eat.

Students open Textbook p. 104–105. The class reads through the section on seasonal foods together, then shifts to the plant-parts categorisation. The teacher draws a simple plant outline on the board — root, stem, leaves, flower, fruit, seed — and children call out examples from the textbook to fill each part.

In notebooks, students write the heading 'Foods from Plants' and list at least two items under each plant part they can remember. They then add a second column 'Foods from Animals' and list milk products, eggs, and meat. The teacher asks: 'Can you think of something we eat that comes from neither a plant nor an animal?' (salt, water) — children discuss.

Students respond to Textbook p. 105 by writing two or three names of crops grown in fields. The teacher invites sharing: 'Which of these crops have you seen growing — in a field, a garden, or a pot at home?' The class closes by noting that food travels from soil, plant, or animal to their plate.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify everyday foods by their natural origin — plant part or animal source — and connect seasonal availability to eating patterns.
periods.section_context: Summer and winter seasonal foods, regional food variety across India, plant-part categories (roots: carrot, radish, beetroot; leaves: spinach, fenugreek, cabbage; fruits: guava, mango; stems: potato, ginger, onion; seeds: grains, pulses), animal-based foods (milk, curd, ghee, eggs, meat), foods from neither plants nor animals (salt, water), field crops.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone know a food that your family makes only in one particular season — why only then?' This surfaces local seasonal and regional practices without labelling them.

periods.activity_title: Drawing Three Thalis and Reflecting on Food Values
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw three plates or thalis with various food items in your notebook (p. 108)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens a brief discussion from Textbook p. 108: 'Why do we need different kinds of food? Why is it important not to waste food?' Children share ideas in pairs, then a few responses are heard aloud. The teacher accepts all thoughtful answers without correcting — the aim is to surface children's own reasoning.

Students draw three thalis in their notebooks — one for the morning meal, one for the afternoon meal, and one for the night meal — following Textbook p. 108. Inside each thali they draw and label the food items their family typically eats at that time. They aim to include variety across plant and animal sources in at least one thali, drawing on the food categories the class explored in earlier work with plant parts and animal foods.

In a gallery-style walk around the room (or sharing with a neighbour), children look at each other's thalis and notice differences: 'Did someone draw a food you have never tried? Did someone include a food from another part of India?' The teacher asks: 'Is there a food on your thali that you think of as special — something your family makes for a particular reason?'

Students write one sentence in their notebook responding to the prompt from Textbook p. 108: 'If a guest came to your home, what food would you serve them and why?' The teacher closes by affirming that sharing food is a way of showing care — and that the great variety in everyone's thalis shows how rich India's food traditions are.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent a varied, balanced set of daily meals through labelled drawings and articulate a food choice with a reason.
periods.section_context: Drawing three thalis for morning, afternoon, and night meals with labelled food items, discussion on food variety and seasonal eating, avoiding food waste, writing a reason for serving a guest a chosen food.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did anyone draw a dish that a grandparent or elder in your family taught you — what makes that dish special to your family?' This draws out food as cultural memory in an unhurried, natural way.

assessment_items.task: Think about a food your family makes at home that you really enjoy. Draw a picture of it in your notebook and write its name. Below the drawing, write two or three words that describe how it looks, smells, or tastes — for example: yellow, sweet, crunchy.
assessment_items.scaffold: My favourite homemade food is: ___________. It looks / smells / tastes: (write 2–3 words) ___________. I like it because: ___________.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any homemade dish the child names — regional and family dishes are all valid. Credit any genuine sensory descriptor (colour, texture, taste, smell). The reason sentence can be simple. Do not expect formal food vocabulary.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express personal food preferences and describe food variety using sensory attributes such as taste, colour, and smell.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can represent a personal food preference through drawing and descriptive language, showing awareness that foods differ in sensory qualities.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides the child through three steps: naming the dish, adding sensory descriptors, and giving a reason. A child who fills all three steps has met the outcome. Sensory words do not need to be 'correct' food-science terms.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: dish is named and drawn recognisably, two or more distinct sensory descriptors are given (not just 'good' or 'nice'), and the reason links to a specific quality. Weak: drawing without a name, or only 'I like it' as the reason with no descriptor.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: A child who cannot write may dictate the words to the teacher or use only the drawing with spoken description. A child who eats only a few foods may describe any of them — variety of dishes across the class is the point, not variety within one child's response.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: labelled drawing with short written descriptors
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing with labelling is the textbook's own mode for this section and is age-appropriate for Grade III, allowing children who are still developing written fluency to demonstrate the outcome.

assessment_items.question_text: Shirin was a runner who often fell sick and performed poorly in races. After talking to her coach, she started eating a greater variety of food every day — vegetables, fruits, different grains, pulses, and nuts. She soon became healthier and ran better. What is the most likely reason her health improved?

options.label: A
options.text: She ate more of her favourite food every day.

options.label: B
options.text: She drank more water but did not change what she ate.

options.label: C
options.text: She started eating many different kinds of food instead of only a few.

options.label: D
options.text: She stopped eating home-cooked food and ate only fruits.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. The story's central lesson is dietary variety, not quantity of a favourite food or a single-food solution.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why eating a variety of food groups contributes to physical well-being, using evidence from a narrative example.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this shows the student conflated eating more with eating better — a common misconception that quantity rather than variety drives health.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this shows the student picked up the word 'fruit' from the balanced-diet list and treated it as the single solution, missing the story's emphasis on variety across food groups.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this shows the student noticed the chapter's hydration message but applied it incorrectly as the sole explanation for Shirin's improvement.

assessment_items.question_text: We eat different foods in summer and in winter. Name one food you or your family eats more in summer and one food you eat more in winter. For each food, write one reason why it suits that season.
expected_elements: A specific food associated with summer (e.g. a cool drink, juicy fruit, or any locally appropriate summer food).
A reason linking the summer food to the season (e.g. it cools us down, it is available in summer, it quenches thirst).
A specific food associated with winter (e.g. a warm soup, stew, or any locally appropriate winter food).
A reason linking the winter food to the season (e.g. it keeps us warm, it is grown in winter, it is available then).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any regionally appropriate foods — there is no single correct answer. In some regions, summer foods may include aam panna, watermelon, or coconut water; winter foods may include til-gur, gajar halwa, or sarson da saag. Credit the reason if it sensibly links the food to the season's characteristics, even if the phrasing is simple.

expected_elements: A specific food associated with summer (e.g. a cool drink, juicy fruit, or any locally appropriate summer food).
A reason linking the summer food to the season (e.g. it cools us down, it is available in summer, it quenches thirst).
A specific food associated with winter (e.g. a warm soup, stew, or any locally appropriate winter food).

assessment_items.task: Draw a thali in your notebook for your afternoon meal. Inside the thali, draw and label at least three food items. Try to include one food that comes from a plant and one that comes from an animal. Below the thali, write one sentence about why it is good to have different kinds of food in one meal.
assessment_items.scaffold: My afternoon thali has: (draw and label 3 or more foods inside the circle). One food from a plant: ___________. One food from an animal: ___________. Having different kinds of food in one meal is good because: ___________.
format_of_output: labelled drawing of a thali with at least three food items
identification of one plant-based and one animal-based food
one sentence explaining the value of variety in a meal
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any combination of foods the child knows — regional and home meals are valid. The thali need not look like a formal plate. Credit any reasonable explanation of variety (e.g. 'so we get different things our body needs', 'so we don't get bored', 'because different foods help us in different ways'). If a child's family is vegetarian, accept a plant-based food for the animal column only if the child explains it comes from an animal product (milk, curd, ghee); otherwise note that the animal-food column may remain a learning point.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent a varied, balanced set of daily meals through labelled drawings and articulate a food choice with a reason.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can construct and label a visual representation of a balanced meal and explain — in simple terms — why variety in food is beneficial.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold moves from drawing to labelling to categorising to reasoning. A child who draws and labels three foods, correctly identifies plant and animal sources for at least one each, and writes any reasonable reason has met the outcome fully.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: thali has three or more recognisable, labelled foods; plant and animal sources are correctly identified; the reason sentence links variety to a concrete benefit (body, health, taste, or need). Weak: unlabelled drawing only, or all items from a single source group with no attempt at variety, or the reason sentence is absent.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: A child who cannot write labels may use spoken labels that the teacher records beside the drawing. A child whose home diet is plant-based may draw all plant foods — the assessment point is variety across plant-part categories, not mandatory animal foods. Accept dictated sentences from children still developing writing fluency.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: labelled drawing with a short written explanation
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The textbook task for this section uses exactly this mode — drawing three thalis — making it the appropriate and authentic form of expression for Grade III children consolidating chapter learning.
